interest: This file offers historians an extraordinary, month-by-month record of Japan’s rapid pivot toward totalitarian political consolidation and Axis alignment during the critical turning point of 1940. It is especially valuable for illustrating how international developments—such as the lapse of the 1911 U.S. commercial treaty and the collapse of France—interacted with severe internal domestic stresses, including critical rice and energy shortages and Diet dissent, to precipitate the fall of the Abe and Yonai cabinets. Furthermore, the inclusion of complete monthly schedules of embassy telegrams and despatches, combined with reporting on specific micro-crises—such as the arrest of foreign journalists, pressure on foreign Christian missions, and military confrontations with U.S. Marines in Shanghai—provides rich evidentiary material on the day-to-day mechanics of prewar American diplomatic observation and reporting.
overview: This file (State Department Record Group 59, decimal file 894.00, File 1247, Part 1) encompasses 560 pages of diplomatic despatches, confidential monthly reports, and Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda generated between January 1940 and February 1941, documenting political, economic, and military conditions in Japan from December 1939 through August 1940. Sent primarily by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and staff at the American Embassy in Tokyo, the collection chronicles the steady deterioration of U.S.–Japanese relations following the expiration and lapse of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation in January 1940, ongoing American protests over property damage in China, the recognition of the Wang Ching-wei regime in Nanking, and localized confrontations like the July 7 Shanghai incident. Concurrently, the reports record Japan’s expanding regional ambitions following the outbreak of the European conflict and the fall of France, detailing pressure exerted on French Indochina and the Netherlands East Indies, Anglo-Japanese disputes over Tientsin and the Burma route, Outer Mongolian border demarcation, and rapprochement efforts with the Soviet Union. Domestically, the documents trace acute wartime distress—including electric power, coal, and rice shortages—and sweeping political upheavals: the collapse of the Abe and Yonai cabinets, Takao Saito’s anti-war speech controversy in the Diet, the formation of Prince Fumimaro Konoye’s second cabinet, the purge of diplomatic personnel under Foreign Minister Matsuoka, and the state-directed mobilization toward the 'New National Structure' (Taisei Yokusankai) and the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere.
